title: Dara and Clef's Echo Game
markdown:
Once, in a calm cave among rolling hills, where wildflowers nodded in a small breeze and the air smelled of moss and sleepy earth, lived Dara the dormouse. She was round as a hazelnut, honey-warm in fur, with eyes like new moons. She loved quiet games and was very good at listening. Sometimes her friend Clef the bat would visit. Clef’s wings were soft as velvet on still water, and he loved to roam the dim rooms of the cave, always hoping to find something new.

One afternoon, as twilight washed the mouth of the cave in lavender and apricot and the crickets began their slow song, Dara said, “Let’s play whispering. You hide, and I will murmur where I think you are.”

Clef fluttered, pleased, and slipped into a shadowy corner, his wingbeats hardly a sound. Dara closed her eyes, breathed in, and whispered, “Clef, are you near the mossy wall?”

No answer came. He was hiding well, still as a shadow.

“Clef, over by the smooth stones?”

Still nothing. She tried a third time, near the little pool that always smelled of rain. “Clef, are you by the water?” The words went out as soft as moth-wing, and the cave kept them. Dara’s murmurs seemed to melt before they reached him. Her whiskers drooped. A tiny sigh left her. Clef, waiting in his corner, felt a small sadness brush his wings, as if he had become a pebble no one would find. He almost called out then, to be kind, but the game had rules, and he loved rules almost as much as flying.

Clef, who always felt the air, tried something else. He stretched his wings in the cool and called a soft “Hoo-hoo” as he glided. The sound travelled, met the solid wall, and whoosh—came home to his own keen ears. It was as if the cave had sent his voice back, a friendly return.

“Hoo-hoo,” he called near another wall of smooth rock. Again the sound came home. Near a big bumpy stone that jutted out, the return arrived quickly, almost like a tap. In the wide-open middle of the cave, it took longer, as if the sound had farther to go. That was when it clicked. The whisper was not lost. It was bouncing.

Clef swooped to Dara, eyes shining. “Dara, the cave is answering me. When I make a sound, it bumps the walls and comes back. It shows me where things are, like a map made of sound.”

Dara tilted her head, ears wide. “Bounces back? Like a little sound-ball playing tag with itself?”

“Yes. Let’s try our game again. You hide, and I will call from different places. Listen for my voice coming home. It will help you find me.”

Dara nestled behind a large smooth stone that felt cool against her fur. Clef flew toward the ceiling and called, “Hoo-hoo. Dara, I am over here.” She closed her eyes. She heard his clear voice, and a moment later a faint hoo-hoo from her left, a hush pointing the way.

“You are to my left, near the wall with the soft drippy water.”

Clef laughed, low and pleased, and moved. “Now where am I?”

Dara waited with her whole small self. The echo came from farther off, softer, as if it had travelled. “Over there,” she said, and pointed.

Clef hid once more, this time high on a ledge where the air was cooler. “Hoo-hoo,” he called, and the return took a slow, sleepy path. Dara did not rush. She let the second sound arrive, then walked toward it, paws quiet on stone, until she found him smiling in the dim. They played a little longer, listening to their voices return through the friendly dark. The finding game was fun again, because the cave would not keep a secret from a careful ear.

Clef landed beside her. “That bouncing sound is called an echo,” he said. “Some bats use echoes to find their way when the world is dim. The wall sends the sound home, and the time it takes tells how near or far.” Dara wondered about owls in the hills, and whether a well would answer a pebble the same way.

Moonlight lay in a pale ribbon at the entrance. They snuggled close, tired and warm. Dara yawned. Clef tucked his head under a wing. The cave held its quiet wonder, and soon, safe in the hush, they drifted into peaceful sleep, while far off the crickets sang, and the walls, if anyone called, would still send the sound home.
